note.note:
Consult Summary:
- Young adult with acute progressive upper lip swelling and respiratory symptoms beginning ~30 minutes after eating prawn soup, concerning for anaphylaxis; ambulance activation and interim antihistamine advised.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Acute swelling of the upper lip (initially left corner), progressive since onset; associated sensation of throat closing, difficulty breathing, and lightheadedness/dizziness.
- Timeline:
  - Ate prawn soup at approximately 7:00 PM.
  - Lip symptoms began about 30 minutes after ingestion and have been worsening since.
  - Patient felt dizzy during the consultation.
  - Patient reports a similar episode ~1 year ago (swelling and difficulty breathing after a late meal) and a severe childhood reaction around age 6.
- Exacerbating / relieving factors:
  - No clear relieving factors reported.
  - Patient instructed to take available antihistamine immediately while awaiting ambulance.
- Associated symptoms / systems review:
  - Respiratory: sensation of decreased ability to breathe, possible chest tightness (patient uncertain).
  - ENT/allergy: progressive lip swelling, reported throat sensation of closing.
  - Neurologic: dizziness/lightheadedness.
  - No reports of rash, hives, vomiting, abdominal pain, syncope, or other localized symptoms in the transcript.
- Pertinent negatives (as stated or not raised):
  - No documented fever, cough (other than breathing difficulty), gastrointestinal symptoms, or documented rash in the transcript.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma.
  - Uses salbutamol inhaler (medication name documented; dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - No other inhalers reported ("no" to additional brown/controller inhalers).
- Known peanut allergy (longstanding).
- Prior severe allergic reaction(s):
  - Childhood episode (~age 6) requiring an injection and reported hospital attendance (per patient/mother recollection).
  - Approximately 1 year prior: swelling and difficulty breathing after eating (details limited), occurred when intoxicated.
- Medications explicitly mentioned:
  - Salbutamol inhaler — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Occasional antihistamines used historically for peanut allergy — specific agent(s) not documented.

Social History:
- Eats out socially with friends; recently tried prawn soup at a restaurant.
- Alcohol: reports being "quite drunk" during prior reaction ~1 year ago (implies prior alcohol use; frequency not documented).
- At start of consultation patient was at home alone; another person arrived during the call (mother present thereafter).

Family History:
- No formal family medical history documented.
- Mother present/available and recalled childhood severe reaction; mother agreed to call emergency services and to provide available antihistamines.

Physical Examination:
- No vital signs documented in the transcript.
- No physical examination findings documented.

Investigations:
- No investigations, imaging, or laboratory results documented.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Suspected anaphylactic reaction (acute allergic reaction to shellfish/prawn suspected)
  - Assessment details:
    - Acute progressive upper lip swelling, throat sensation of closing, respiratory difficulty, and dizziness beginning ~30 minutes after prawn ingestion — clinically concerning for anaphylaxis.
    - History of prior severe allergic reactions (childhood injection/hospitalization; prior episode ~1 year ago).
  - Plan items:
    - Ambulance/emergency services to be contacted for immediate assessment and treatment (doctor recommended ambulance; patient’s mother agreed to call emergency services — 999).
    - Interim: take any available oral antihistamine immediately while awaiting ambulance (patient instructed to do so; mother reported antihistamines available).
    - Ensure someone stays with patient until ambulance arrives.
    - Ambulance/hospital may administer intramuscular adrenaline if indicated (doctor explained injection may be required).
    - Advise attendance to hospital for observation and definitive management.
    - After hospital discharge, follow-up with the clinic to arrange review and discussion about injectable adrenaline/autoinjector and allergy management (doctor requested patient to call back after hospital).
- Issue 2: Asthma (background condition)
  - Assessment details:
    - Documented history of asthma; patient uses salbutamol inhaler.
    - No current inhaler use during event documented.
  - Plan items:
    - No specific acute asthma treatment documented in the consult beyond emergency services; asthma history noted for emergency responders and hospital team.
- Issue 3: Known peanut allergy and prior anaphylaxis risk / need for allergist follow-up and adrenaline autoinjector
  - Assessment details:
    - Longstanding peanut allergy; prior severe childhood reaction requiring injection and hospital attendance.
  - Plan items:
    - Recommend hospital/allergy clinic assessment post-acute event to determine need for prescription of intramuscular adrenaline autoinjector and specialist referral (doctor indicated they may need to "sort you out" with injections after hospital).

General plan items:
- Patient instructed to take available antihistamine now while awaiting emergency services.
- Patient to have someone stay with her until ambulance arrives.
- Patient to attend hospital for assessment; to contact clinic after hospital discharge for further management regarding adrenaline autoinjector/allergy follow-up.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No vital signs recorded (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure).
  - No physical examination documented (airway, respiratory exam, skin exam for urticaria/angioedema).
  - No documentation of medication doses/routes/frequency for salbutamol or any antihistamine.
  - No documentation of whether patient administered any emergency medication (e.g., intramuscular epinephrine) prior to arrival.
  - No allergy list with exact reactions/severity beyond patient's statements.
  - No documentation of whether ambulance was actually dispatched by clinician or only by patient’s mother.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Initial notes referenced a "sandwich," but patient clarified the trigger was prawn soup — conflict noted between initial record and patient history.
  - Doctor stated he would call an ambulance, later instructed mother to call 999; final ambulance dispatch status not explicitly documented — conflict/uncertainty noted.
- Transcript quality:
  - Overall consultation content understandable; occasional brief interruptions and some incomplete phrases by patient (e.g., uncertainty about specific antihistamine names).
  - No objective exam data or vitals available in transcript.
